components.name: Avatar
components.title: Avatar
components.summary: A small square that shows who someone is. The name is required, because it's both the alt text (the description screen readers read for an image) and the source of the initials. Without one, an avatar is just an image nobody can identify.
components.useWhen: Showing who a person is, next to their name, as in a roster row, a comment or an account menu.
components.notFor: Several people in one spot: use AvatarGroup.

props.name: name
props.description: Required. The source of the fallback initials and the announced name.

props.name: src
props.description: Optional image. If it can't load, the fallback takes its place without the layout jumping.

props.name: status
props.description: Whether the person is around. It adds the dot and adds the word to the announced name. Leave it out when you don't know.

props.name: className
props.description: Merged with the component's classes. When Tailwind utility classes clash, the later one wins.

props.name: ref
props.description: Passed through to the root element.

props.name: ...rest
props.description: Every native span prop except aria-label and children. aria-label is removed from the types rather than quietly overwritten when the page runs. The announced name comes from the sr-only span, and an aria-label on the root would override it. children is removed because the component renders its own image/fallback/sr-only children, so anything passed as children would silently disappear.

api.name: AvatarStatus
api.code:
/** Every native span prop except `aria-label` is available — a molecule composing an Avatar can
 *  attach a `data-testid` or extra `aria-*`/`data-*` attributes. `aria-label` is typed `never`
 *  rather than merely omitted: Avatar's whole guarantee is that the announced name comes from the
 *  `sr-only` span's content and is identical whether or not the image loads. An `aria-label` on
 *  the root would silently outrank that content-derived name in the accessibility tree (an
 *  element's `aria-label` always wins over its text content when the accessible name is
 *  computed), defeating the one thing this component promises. `Omit<>` alone is a no-op here —
 *  TypeScript's JSX checker never treats an `aria-*`/`data-*`-prefixed attribute as an
 *  excess/unknown property — so the key must be redeclared with type `never` to actually be
 *  enforced. Same remedy as `IconButton`'s `aria-label` exclusion (see `IconButton.tsx`).
 *
 *  `children` is excluded for a plainer reason: `HTMLAttributes` offers it, but this component
 *  renders its own image/fallback/`sr-only` children, so JSX children on the element always win
 *  and a `children` prop is silently discarded — reachable, typed, and dead. It is an ordinary
 *  key, so the `Omit` does the rejecting and the declared `never` only makes the error legible;
 *  both are shipped, matching `IconButton`. */
export type AvatarStatus = 'online' | 'away' | 'busy' | 'offline'

dos: Pass the full name, not the initials. The component works those out itself.
Let it fall back. The fallback is part of the design, not an error state.
Use sm inside dense rows and tables.
Set status only where presence is live and matters (a roster, a chat). A dot that's out of date is worse than no dot.
donts: Don't round it. The system has no round corners, and an avatar isn't the place to start.
Don't add the cut corner to the sm avatar. It's 24px, the same size Kbd leaves out by name. An 8px cut takes a third of that edge, and it looks like a broken square instead of a shaped one.
Don't build an overlapping stack by hand. AvatarGroup does it, with a '+N' that's real text.
Don't explain the dot colours only in a legend. The status word is already in the name, so show it as text where sighted users need it too.
Don't use an avatar as the only label for a person. Put the name next to it in dense UI (user interface).
Don't pass aria-label. It's removed from the types so nothing can override it, and name already decides the one label that gets announced.

anatomy.description: A border.hairline-strong edge on the sunken surface, with overflow clipped and a cut bottom-right corner at md and lg.
alt is empty on purpose, because the hidden name already does the announcing.

Initials worked out from the name, aria-hidden, shown when there's no image or it fails to load. aria-hidden is an ARIA attribute (Accessible Rich Internet Applications, the labels that tell screen readers what things are) that hides something from screen readers.
sr-only (visible to screen readers only) and always there, so the announcement is the same either way. With a status it reads "Ilse Varga, online".

Optional. A square in the top-right corner (the bottom-right is the cut), in accent.ok.text, accent.warning.text, accent.hostile.text or text.muted, with a 2px (pixel) surface.base keyline around it. It's aria-hidden because the status is announced in the name.

components.name: Badge
components.title: Badge
components.summary: A small chip that shows a status. It comes in six tones and two emphases, and it always carries a word. A colour on its own isn't a status anyone can read.
components.useWhen: You need to label a status with a word and a tone, like an order state or a sync result.
components.notFor: A filter or selection someone can remove. Use Tag for that.

props.name: tone
props.description: The status the badge shows.

props.name: emphasis
props.description: Solid uses the invariant fill (the same in light and dark themes) with its matching ink. Subtle is the outline badge: a 1px border and text in the tone’s theme-adaptive text token, with no fill. There's no separate outline emphasis, because it would be this same look under a second name.

props.name: size
props.description: sm (small) is the chip for everyday interface: rows, cards, tables. md (medium) takes the small control height (32px) and the 14px text step. Use it for a badge next to display-size type, like a price.

props.name: dot
props.description: Adds a marker next to the text.

props.name: icon
props.description: An icon before the text, hidden from screen readers with aria-hidden and sized to the badge. It takes the badge’s colour, so the same contrast pair that covers the text covers it too. It adds to the word. It never replaces it.

props.name: className
props.description: Merged with the component classes. If two clash, the later Tailwind utility wins (Tailwind is the CSS framework this system styles with).

props.name: ref
props.description: Passed through to the span element.

props.name: ...rest
props.description: Any other span attribute. For example, aria-hidden on a count that a label next to it already reads out.

api.code: export const badgeVariants = cva( …

dos: Give every badge a word.
Go easy on solid. One solid badge in a row reads as the exception. Six read as noise.
Keep the tone mapping the same across the product. ok is never ‘in progress’ on one screen and ‘done’ on another.
Use size md when the badge sits next to a headline figure, so the two read as one statement.
donts: Don't build a badge that's colour only, even with a tooltip.
Don't put a badge inside a button. It muddies what the clickable target is.
Don't use hostile for something that's only pending.
Don't bevel it (give it a cut corner). At 22px a badge is chrome, the frame around content, not an object with its own footprint. Kbd follows the same rule for the same reason.
Don't resize a badge with height or text classes. The two sizes are the prop. A third size is a change to the system.
Don't use size md in a table row or on a card. It's as tall as a small button, so it starts to look like one.
Don't give one badge both an icon and a dot. Pick one marker. Two say the same thing twice.
Don't colour the icon yourself. It inherits the badge’s tone, and that's the pair the contrast gate (the automated colour-contrast check) measures.

anatomy.description: Set in mono (a fixed-width typeface), uppercase. That's the tertiary type role. By default it's 22px tall with 11px text (px means pixels); at size md it's 32px tall with 14px text.

Optional, and placed before the text. It's aria-hidden (an ARIA attribute, from Accessible Rich Internet Applications, that hides it from screen readers) and uses the current text colour. It's 12px, or 14px at size md.
An optional square, also aria-hidden, in the current text colour. It's 6px, or 8px at size md.
Required. The word is what makes the badge accessible.

components.name: Button
components.title: Button
components.summary: The main control for taking an action. It comes in five variants (one of them a button that looks like a text link) and four sizes, with optional icons on either side of the label. It also draws its own focus ring, the outline that shows which control the keyboard is on. The component places that ring for you, because the bevel (the cut corners) would clip one placed anywhere else.
components.useWhen: An action on this page, like submit, save or open a dialog.
components.notFor: Going somewhere (use Link, or Button asChild around an anchor), or an action with no visible word (use IconButton).

props.name: variant
props.description: Which fill/border treatment to use. link looks like a Link (signal text, underline, no fill, no bevel, no fixed height) but it's still a button. Use it for an action inside a sentence, not for going to another page.

props.name: size
props.description: 24 / 32 / 40 / 48px (pixels). xs is exactly the 24px minimum target, the smallest area people can reliably click or tap. It isn't a token step (there is no xs control-height token) and it's meant for dense toolbars and table rows. Size has no effect on the link variant, which takes the size of the text around it.

props.name: fullWidth
props.description: Stretches the wrapper as well as the button.

props.name: loading
props.description: Sets aria-busy and aria-disabled, blocks the click and the form submit, and shows the spinner. The button stays focusable.

props.name: loadingLabel
props.description: Text that's hidden on screen but read aloud while loading.

props.name: iconStart
props.description: An icon before the label, rendered aria-hidden and sized to the button. The spinner replaces it while loading. It isn't available with asChild: put the icon inside the child element instead.

props.name: iconEnd
props.description: An icon after the label, rendered aria-hidden. It stays while loading. Not available with asChild.

props.name: asChild
props.description: Renders the child element with the button's classes. Use it for links that look like buttons. Combining it with disabled, loading or loadingLabel is a type error, so the code won't compile, instead of quietly doing nothing. A link can't really be disabled or made busy, so those props are removed from the types rather than ignored when the page runs.

props.name: wrapperClassName
props.description: Classes for the focus wrapper, not the button.

props.name: className
props.description: Merged with the component's classes. When Tailwind utility classes clash, the later one wins.

props.name: ref
props.description: Passed through to the button element.

props.name: type
props.description: A Button never submits a form by accident. Ask for submit on the one that should.

props.name: ...rest
props.description: Every native button prop except aria-busy. aria-busy is removed from the types rather than quietly overwritten when the page runs. loading is the only thing that sets it, and a loading button saying aria-busy="false" would be a spinning, aria-disabled control telling assistive tech (screen readers and other tools people with disabilities use) that it's idle. children is its own declared prop above, not part of rest.

api.name: buttonVariants
api.code: export const buttonVariants = cva( …

keyboard.does: Moves focus to the button. The ring appears on the wrapper.
Activates it. While loading it does nothing, and the caller's onClick doesn't run.
Activates it. While loading it does nothing, and the caller's onClick doesn't run.

dos: One primary button per view. The signal colour only means something if it's rare.
Use asChild for a link that should look like a button, so it stays a real link.
Say what the button does: ‘Dispatch team’, not ‘Submit’.
Use loading instead of disabling the button and swapping the label yourself.
Use loading on a submit button. It keeps focus while the form works, so a keyboard user is never thrown back to the top of the page.
Pass icons through iconStart and iconEnd, not as children. That way they stay hidden from assistive tech and get sized with the button.
Use the link variant for an action that sits in running text or next to a heading (‘Reset filters’). Use Link for anything that goes somewhere.
donts: Don't add bevel-* or an outline class yourself. You'll clip the ring off.
Don't use danger for anything that can be undone.
Don't put a ghost button next to a secondary one. People can't tell which matters more any more.
Don't disable a button without saying somewhere why it's disabled.
Don't use the link variant to go to another page. A control that goes somewhere is a Link, or a Button with asChild around an anchor.
Don't make an icon-only button by passing iconStart with no label. That's IconButton, which requires a name.
Don't use xs for a page's main actions. It's the minimum target size, for dense rows only.
Don't try to disable a link (asChild) or give it a loading state. Render the state you want directly instead (a plain span, or a real disabled button) rather than fighting the type error.

pitfalls.why: Buttons render inline-flex, and JSX (the HTML-like syntax React components are written in) drops the whitespace between them, so buttons placed side by side touch. The parent sets the gap. npm run check:button-spacing fails if there isn't one.
A busy button stays focusable and tells people it's busy through loading. Native disabled is for an action that isn't available, and it takes the button out of the tab order, so the Tab key skips it.

anatomy.description: A span that isn't clipped, carrying .bevel-focus-wrap. It draws the ring on :has(:focus-visible), so a mouse click doesn't show it, plus the reticle brackets (corner marks like a targeting sight) that close in on hover. It's always there and never optional.
The clipped, bevelled control. It never carries its own outline.
Decoration only, shown while loading. The hidden label is what screen readers announce.
Oxanium semibold, uppercase: the display type role. The link variant switches to the body role, in the signal text colour, underlined.

Optional, before and after the label. Each sits in an aria-hidden slot sized to the button (14px at xs and sm, 16px at md, 20px at lg). aria-hidden is an ARIA attribute (Accessible Rich Internet Applications, the labels that tell screen readers what things are) that hides the icon from screen readers. While loading, the spinner takes the leading slot.

components.name: Checkbox
components.title: Checkbox
components.summary: A checkbox with three states: off, on and mixed. Radix (the open-source library of accessible building blocks underneath it) handles the semantics and the keyboard behaviour. The look comes from the system's shape language: a square with no rounding and a tick in ink.
components.useWhen: An on/off choice that applies when the form is saved, or a parent whose children are partly selected.
components.notFor: A setting that takes effect the moment you flip it. Use Switch for that.

props.name: checked
props.description: The checked state, when your code controls it.

props.name: defaultChecked
props.description: The starting state when the checkbox manages itself (uncontrolled). It's narrower than Radix's own boolean | 'indeterminate'. The tick or dash can only follow a checked value the caller passed in. Radix would track an uncontrolled mixed state internally but never hand it back, so that state is excluded instead of being drawn with the wrong mark.

props.name: onCheckedChange
props.description: Runs every time it toggles.

props.name: disabled
props.description: Takes it out of the tab order and stops it toggling.

props.name: required
props.description: Uses the browser's built-in form validation.

props.name: name
props.description: The field name sent with a native form.

props.name: value
props.description: The field value sent with a native form.

props.name: invalid
props.description: Sets aria-invalid (an ARIA attribute, from Accessible Rich Internet Applications, that tells screen readers the field has an error) and shows the invalid border.

props.name: id
props.description: Pair it with a real label through htmlFor.

props.name: className
props.description: Merged with the control's classes. If two clash, the later Tailwind utility wins (Tailwind is the CSS framework this system styles with).

props.name: ref
props.description: Passed through to the Radix root button.

props.name: ...rest
props.description: Every Radix Checkbox.Root prop except aria-invalid, spread onto the root. aria-invalid is removed from the type, so you can't pass it, instead of being quietly overwritten while the page runs. invalid is the only thing that sets both the attribute and the border. defaultChecked is declared again above, narrowed to boolean.

keyboard.does: Moves focus to it.
Toggles it.
Nothing. That's how a native checkbox behaves, so it isn't a bug to fix.

dos: Give it a real <label htmlFor>, or let FormField do it.
Use the mixed state for a parent whose children are partly selected.
Put the label on the right and make it part of the clickable target.
donts: Don't use a checkbox for something that takes effect right away. That's a Switch.
Don't rely on the fill colour alone. The tick and the dash are what show the state.
Don't nest checkbox groups more than one level deep.

anatomy.description: A button with role=checkbox, which tells screen readers it's a checkbox. A native input can't be styled this way. The box is 20px (pixels) and the hit area, the part you can click or tap, is 24px.
A tick when checked, a dash when mixed. The shape changes, so the state never depends on colour alone.
A ::before inset of -2px, which clears the 24×24 minimum in WCAG 2.2 (the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, the public rulebook for making websites usable by people with disabilities).

components.name: Divider
components.title: Divider
components.summary: A thin line, with an optional legend (a short text label). When it's only decoration, screen readers skip it. When it marks where a section starts, it's a real separator they announce.
components.useWhen: A thin line between groups of content, labelled when it starts a new section.
components.notFor: Making space (use the spacing scale), or going between items that already have their own borders.

props.name: orientation
props.description: Which way the line runs.

props.name: label
props.description: Adds a legend and makes the divider more than decoration.

props.name: className
props.description: Merged with the component's classes. When Tailwind utility classes clash, the later one wins.

props.name: ref
props.description: Passed through to the root element.

props.name: ...rest
props.description: Every native div prop except role and children. role is removed from the types rather than quietly overwritten when the page runs, because label already decides whether the divider is decorative or structural. children is removed because it behaved two different ways: with no label it rendered inside a decorative separator, and with one it disappeared.

dos: Leave it decorative when it's only there for visual rhythm.
Label it when it really starts a new section, so screen readers announce the structure.
Add anim-draw-on when a section animates in. The line drawing itself is motion token M2.
donts: Don't stack dividers to make space. That's what the spacing scale is for.
Don't label every divider. If everything is a landmark, nothing is.
Don't use a vertical divider between items that already have their own borders.
Don't pass role. It's removed from the types so nothing can override it, and label already decides none vs separator.

anatomy.description: 1px (one pixel) in border.hairline.
JetBrains Mono, 10px, muted. Optional.
none when decorative, separator when labelled. role tells screen readers what an element is.

components.name: IconButton
components.title: Icon button
components.summary: A square button with one icon. It uses exactly the same variants as Button (same source code, so the two can't drift apart). It requires a label, because an icon on its own tells a screen reader nothing.
components.useWhen: An action shown as a single icon, with a label that names the action.
components.notFor: An action with a visible word (use Button), or a status (use Badge).

props.name: label
props.description: Required. It becomes aria-label. It's required in the types, so an icon button with no name won't compile.

props.name: variant
props.description: Which fill/border treatment to use. These are Button’s variants minus link, since an icon has no text to underline.

props.name: size
props.description: 32 / 40 / 48px (pixels), all above the 24px minimum target size, the smallest area people can reliably click or tap. Button’s xs isn't offered: 32px is the smallest this control goes.

props.name: count
props.description: A number in a corner badge, like items in a cart or unread notifications. It's added to the accessible name, the name screen readers announce (‘Notifications, 3 unread’). It shows as 99+ past 99 and is hidden at 0 unless showZero is set.

props.name: countLabel
props.description: Formats the spoken part of the name that comes after the label and a comma: count => `${count} unread`. It always gets the real number, never 99+.

props.name: showZero
props.description: Shows the badge when the count is 0.

props.name: asChild
props.description: Renders the child element with the button's classes. Use it for links that look like icon buttons. Combining it with disabled is a type error, so the code won't compile, instead of quietly doing nothing. A link can't really be disabled, so the prop is removed from the types rather than ignored when the page runs.

props.name: fullWidth
props.description: Left out on purpose. An icon button is always square, and stretching it would break that.

props.name: wrapperClassName
props.description: Classes for the focus wrapper, not the button.

props.name: className
props.description: Merged with the component's classes. When Tailwind utility classes clash, the later one wins.

props.name: ref
props.description: Passed through to the button element.

props.name: ...rest
props.description: Every native button prop except aria-label. aria-label is removed from the types rather than quietly overwritten when the page runs. label is the only source of the accessible name, and an aria-label in rest would beat it. children is its own declared prop above, not part of rest.

keyboard.does: Moves focus to the button. The ring appears on the wrapper.
Activates it.
Activates it.

dos: Make the label describe the action, not the icon: ‘Dismiss alert’, not ‘X’.
Mark the icon aria-hidden so it's never announced twice.
Pair it with a Tooltip when the icon's meaning isn't obvious.
Stick to one icon. Two icons in a square is a dropdown, not a button.
Give a count a countLabel that says what's being counted, so the name reads ‘Notifications, 3 unread’ and not just a number.
donts: Don't ship an icon button that only regular users understand.
Don't go smaller than sm. 32px is already close to the 24px floor.
Don't use danger for a dismiss. Dismissing can be undone.
Don't put the count in the label yourself. Pass count, so the badge and the name always match.
Don't use a count for a status (online, error). A count is a number. A status is a Badge with a word.
Don't try to disable a link (asChild). Render the state you want directly instead (a plain span, or a real disabled icon button) rather than fighting the type error.

anatomy.description: A span that isn't clipped, carrying .bevel-focus-wrap. It draws the focus ring (the outline that shows which control the keyboard is on) on :has(:focus-visible), so a mouse click doesn't show it, plus the reticle brackets (corner marks like a targeting sight) that close in on hover. It's always there and never optional.
Its width is pinned to the height token, and the padding is removed.

Always aria-hidden, an ARIA attribute (Accessible Rich Internet Applications, the labels that tell screen readers what things are) that hides it from screen readers. The label gives the button its name.

components.name: Input
components.title: Input
components.summary: A single-line text field. It doesn't label itself. The label, help text, error text and the wiring between them are FormField's job. On its own, Input handles the box, its states and the focus ring (the outline that shows which element the keyboard is on). It also has three optional extras inside its right edge: a password reveal, a character counter and a clear button.
components.useWhen: Single-line text, inside a FormField.
components.notFor: Several lines of text: use Textarea. Searching the page: use Search.
requires: A <FormField> around it. On its own the control has no label. FormField adds the label, the help text and the error, and connects their ids.

props.name: inputSize
props.description: Called inputSize because size is already a real HTML attribute on input.

props.name: invalid
props.description: Sets aria-invalid (an ARIA attribute, from Accessible Rich Internet Applications, that tells screen readers the field has an error) and shows the invalid border. It doesn't show any error text.

props.name: size
props.description: The browser's own attribute, still available.

props.name: revealable
props.description: On type="password", adds a Show password toggle with aria-pressed. The name stays the same, and the pressed state says whether the password is showing. It goes back to hidden when the form submits. Other types ignore it.

props.name: showCount
props.description: Works with maxLength. It shows 12/80 in mono inside the field and adds it to aria-describedby, the attribute that links extra description to a field. It's merged with any describedby you pass in, which is how FormField keeps its help and error text. It only announces the characters left near the limit (the last tenth, and at least the last three), through a polite live region, an area screen readers read out without interrupting.

props.name: clearable
props.description: Shows a clear button while the field has a value (never when it's disabled or read-only). Clearing fires onChange with an empty value, so a controlled field clears through its own handler. Then it calls onClear, then puts focus back in the input.

props.name: onClear
props.description: Called after the clear button empties the field.

props.name: clearLabel
props.description: The clear button’s name. If the page has more than one, say what it clears: ‘Clear call sign’.

props.name: wrapperClassName
props.description: Classes for the wrapper a field with extras renders. Put width classes here when an extra is on. It does nothing on a bare input.

props.name: className
props.description: Merged with the input’s classes. If two clash, the later Tailwind utility wins (Tailwind is the CSS framework this system styles with).

props.name: ref
props.description: Passed through to the input element.

props.name: ...rest
props.description: Every native input prop except aria-invalid, spread onto the element. aria-invalid is removed from the type, so you can't pass it, instead of being quietly overwritten while the page runs. invalid is the only thing that sets both the attribute and the border. If a caller could set one directly, what you see and what screen readers hear could drift apart. size is declared again above as the native number attribute, because inputSize controls the variant.

api.name: inputVariants
api.code: export const inputVariants = cva( …

keyboard.does: Moves focus to the input, then to its clear button and reveal toggle if they are there.
Nothing by default, even with clearable. Clearing on Escape is a search behaviour, and it lives in the Search molecule.
On the reveal toggle, shows or hides the password. On the clear button, empties the field and puts focus back in it.

dos: Label it: with a real <label> today, and with FormField once that ships.
Set the right type and autocomplete. They do more for usability than any styling here.
Pair invalid with visible error text that the input points to through aria-describedby.
Size the field to the expected input. A four-digit code doesn't need a full-width box.
Use showCount with maxLength instead of building a counter next to the field. You get the describedby wiring and the near-limit announcement for free.
Label a field with extras through FormField or a label htmlFor, never a label wrapped around it. A wrapping label pulls the clear and reveal buttons into the field’s name.
donts: Don't use the placeholder as the label. It disappears the moment someone types.
Don't bevel it. A cut corner on a 40px box looks like damage, and it would clip the focus ring.
Don't set invalid without saying what's wrong.
Don't disable a field to make it read-only. Use readOnly, which you can still focus and copy from.
Don't add clearable to a search field. Search already has its own clear button and the Escape key.
Don't build your own show-password button next to a revealable field. You'll end up with two.

anatomy.description: 40px (pixels) tall by default. The height comes from the control token, not a hand-picked number.
border.control at rest, text.muted on hover and hostile.text when invalid. A control's edge tells you something, it isn't decoration, so it doesn't use a hairline token.
Drawn on the input itself. Form controls aren't bevelled (given a cut corner), so nothing clips it.

Optional extras inside the right edge, in this order: the count in mono (a fixed-width typeface), the clear button and the reveal toggle. Turning on any of them wraps the input in a relative box (wrapperClassName styles it) and sizes the right padding to fit them, so text never runs underneath. With none on, the input is bare, with no wrapper.
text.placeholder, with contrast measured against the control fill it sits on, not the page. It's never a stand-in for a label.

components.notFor: Anything that isn't a key, such as a status: use Badge.

components.name: Link
components.title: Link
components.summary: A link inside text. It's underlined, because in a paragraph colour alone isn't enough to show that something is a link.
components.useWhen: Text that takes you somewhere: another page, a section or another site.
components.notFor: Something that does an action. Use Button for that (its link variant if it's inside running text).

props.description: Which colour treatment to use.

props.name: external
props.description: Opens the link in a new tab. It adds target="_blank", the rel hardening (attributes that stop the new page reaching back into yours), a trailing icon and the hidden "(opens in a new tab)" warning. Using it together with target or rel is a type error, so it can't fail silently. external already sets those values, so those props are removed from the type instead of being quietly overwritten while the page runs.

props.name: href
props.description: Where the link goes.

props.name: className
props.description: Merged with the component classes. If two clash, the later Tailwind utility wins (Tailwind is the CSS framework this system styles with).

props.name: ref
props.description: Passed through to the anchor element.

props.name: ...rest
props.description: Every native anchor prop.

api.name: linkVariants

Follows the link.

Set external on anything that leaves the app, so screen readers announce the new tab.
Use quiet in dense lists where every row is a link anyway.

Don't open a new tab without external. The rel hardening and the warning both come with it.
Don't remove the underline to make a paragraph look tidier.
Don't pass target or rel together with external. Those props are removed from the type, so you can't override them. If you need different values, render a plain anchor yourself.

1px (pixel) thick, sitting 2px below the text. It gets thicker on hover in the signal tone.
Hidden from screen readers with aria-hidden (an ARIA attribute, from Accessible Rich Internet Applications). It only shows when external is set.

components.name: LoadingAnimation
components.title: Loading animation
components.summary: A loading state that fills a whole panel, drawn as an animated instrument dial in WebGL (the browser's graphics engine for drawing with the graphics card). The three dials follow the same rules. They draw themselves from the outside in, and their structure drifts. One mechanism clicks to its next detent using the system's snap easing (the motion where things arrive a little large and settle), and the signal accent colour only appears on the part that shows progress.
components.useWhen: A wait that takes over a whole panel or page, like a route loading, a report building or a first sync.
components.notFor: A wait inside a button or a line of text: use Spinner. A wait with a known end: use Progress.

props.name: variant
props.description: Aperture: shaded blades stepping round a spinning core. Gyro: nested rings turning against each other. Reticle: a progress ring filling up from a marker at 12 o’clock.

props.name: size
props.description: A 96px, 160px or 240px square (px means pixels). It shrinks with its container below that size, but never grows.

props.name: label
props.description: Status text that is hidden on screen. Passing it turns the loader into a live region, an area screen readers announce when it changes.

props.name: className
props.description: Merged with the component classes. If two clash, the later Tailwind utility wins (Tailwind is the CSS framework this system styles with).

props.name: ref
props.description: Passed through to the root div.

props.name: ...rest
props.description: Every native div prop except role, for the same reason as Spinner: label is the only thing that sets role="status".

dos: Use it for a wait that takes over a panel or a page, like a route loading, a report building or a first sync.
Pass label, and say what is loading: ‘Loading field kits’, not ‘Loading’.
Pick one dial for each product surface and stick with it. The three are a family. They aren't meant to rotate.
donts: Don't put it in a button or a line of text. That's Spinner, which doesn't use up a WebGL context.
Don't show more than a handful at once. Each one uses a WebGL context (one slot of the browser's graphics engine), and browsers cap how many you get.
Don't rely on the motion. When someone has reduced motion turned on, it shows one still frame, so the label has to carry the meaning.
Don't use it for a wait with a known end. That's Progress.

anatomy.description: The root: a square box at the size you pick. It gets role="status", which makes screen readers announce it, only when it has a label.
A layer that holds the WebGL canvas, hidden from screen readers with aria-hidden (an ARIA attribute, from Accessible Rich Internet Applications). It fades in once the first frame is drawn.
Rings, tick crowns and arcs in text.primary, text.secondary, border.control and border.hairline.strong. One moving part is in accent.signal.fill.
If WebGL isn't available, the Conveyor spinner shows in the same box. It's aria-hidden, so the label is still read only once.
The text screen readers announce (sr-only means it's for screen readers only). It's only there when you pass label.

components.name: Progress
components.title: Progress
components.summary: A progress bar that's either determinate (it knows how far along the task is) or indeterminate (it doesn't). The readout is real text in the DOM (the Document Object Model, the live page structure the browser builds) from the very first render. That's motion token M3's rule, and it means a screen reader, the software that reads the page aloud for blind and low-vision people, never hears a number roll.
components.useWhen: Showing how far a measurable task has got. Switch to indeterminate once you no longer know how much is left.
components.notFor: A wait with no measurable work. Use Spinner.

props.name: label
props.description: Required. The bar’s accessible name.

props.name: value
props.description: null means indeterminate. The value is clamped to [0, max], so an out-of-range value shows as complete instead of overflowing the track.

props.name: max
props.description: The value at which the bar is complete.

props.name: showValue
props.description: Shows the percentage (or "In progress") as a readout.

props.name: tone
props.description: The fill colour. signal paints accent.signal.fill to match Slider. On the track in light theme that’s a 2.15:1 contrast ratio, below the 3:1 a bar needs when it’s the only sign of progress. So set showValue there.

props.name: className
props.description: Merged with the outer wrapper’s classes. Later Tailwind utilities (Tailwind is the CSS framework the system is styled with) win.

props.name: ref
props.description: Passed through to the Radix Progress root, which is the bar itself. Radix is the library of accessible building blocks this component sits on.

props.name: ...rest
props.description: Every native div prop except children, spread onto the outer wrapper, so a molecule can attach a data-testid there. children is typed away because this component draws its own label row and track, and a children prop would be thrown away without any warning.

dos: Name what’s progressing, not the act of progressing.
Use showValue whenever the number itself is useful to the reader.
Switch to null the moment you stop knowing how much is left. Don’t freeze at 90%.
donts: Don't animate the number up from zero and call that animated value the readout. The real value belongs in the DOM straight away.
Don't use Progress for a wait with no measurable work. That's a Spinner.
Don't put the padded readout into the accessible name. That's exactly why the pad is a separate aria-hidden span, and label is what Radix announces.
Don't rely on the tone alone to say something failed. Say it in text.

anatomy.description: Required. Set in mono (a monospaced font, where every character is the same width) and uppercase. It’s also the bar’s accessible name, the name assistive tech such as a screen reader announces for it.
Optional, and the star of the row: 24px (pixels) Oxanium against an 11px label. It uses tabular figures, digits that all take the same width, so the number doesn’t jitter as it changes.

These are padding, not part of the value. They’re dimmed to numeral.pad and marked aria-hidden (an ARIA attribute, from Accessible Rich Internet Applications, that hides an element from assistive tech). So the readout keeps a fixed three-digit width, while a screen reader still hears 40%, not zero four zero percent.
6px tall, a sunken surface, no border. It’s the same track as Slider.
It’s moved rather than resized. That way the browser animates a transform, which is cheap, instead of recalculating the layout.

Selects the next option.

components.name: Select
components.title: Select
components.summary: A single choice from a list, shown in a portalled listbox (a pop-up list rendered at the top level of the page, so nothing around it can clip it). Options come in as an array instead of as children, because the trigger, the panel and the look of each row are decisions the system makes once, not per use.
components.useWhen: One choice from a list of about five options or more.
components.notFor: Several values: use MultiSelect. Fewer than about five options: use Radio.
requires: A <FormField> around it. On its own the control has no label. FormField supplies the label, the help text and the error, and connects their ids so assistive tech (screen readers and similar tools) reads them together.

props.name: label
props.description: Required. The trigger’s accessible name, the name a screen reader announces for it.

props.name: options
props.description: { value, label, disabled?, icon? } rows shown in the listbox. Pass this or groups, never both.

props.name: groups
props.description: { label, options }[]: rows under headings. Pass this or options, never both.

props.name: placeholder
props.description: Shown until a value is chosen.

props.name: value
props.description: The selection, when you control it from outside. Following Radix’s own convention, pass it together with onValueChange.

props.name: defaultValue
props.description: The starting selection, when the select manages it itself (uncontrolled). Pass this or value, never both.

props.name: onValueChange
props.description: Fires with the new value when a row is chosen, whether the select is controlled or uncontrolled.

Opens the listbox.

dos: Keep option labels short and written the same way.
Use a placeholder that says what’s being chosen.
Disable an unavailable option instead of removing it, so the list stops jumping around.
Below about five options, use radios instead.
Group rows under headings once the list mixes different kinds of thing, and keep each group to a handful.
Give every row an icon, or none of them.
Wrap it in a FormField for a visible label, help and error. FormField hands it the label.
donts: Don't build a searchable select out of this. That's the command palette's job.
Don't use it for several values. That's MultiSelect, which shows each choice as a removable tag.
Don't put more than a couple of dozen options in it without search.
Don't make a group of one. A heading over a single row is just noise.
Don't style the trigger differently from Input. A form with mismatched control heights looks broken.

Don't bevel the trigger. It shares Input's frame and draws its own focus ring (the outline that shows which control the keyboard is on), and a cut corner would clip it. The listbox carries the crosshair instead: the shape lives on the surface, not on the control.
Don't pass aria-label or aria-invalid through triggerProps. Both are typed away, not overridable, because label and invalid already decide them.

anatomy.description: Uses exactly the same frame and styling as Input, so a select and a text field line up in a form.
Shows the placeholder until something’s chosen.

Portalled and positioned by Radix, the library of accessible building blocks this sits on. It slides down out of the trigger as it opens (M7; Radix’s Select closes at once, with no exit animation). It’s the one atom that carries the corner crosshair, because it’s a surface framing other content, and that’s what the crosshair marks. It’s also the shape that can’t be cut, since clip-path would clip the crosshair’s arms and the last row’s selection fill along with them.
Highlighted rows use signal.fill with signal.ink. That’s the fill-selection grammar, the system’s rule for how a selection looks.
A tick on the selected row, so selection isn’t shown by the highlight alone.

Optional. Sits before the label and is aria-hidden, an ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications) attribute that hides it from assistive tech. It follows the row colour, so it turns ink on the highlight. It isn’t shown in the trigger.
Used with groups: a mono (monospaced font) heading over its rows that names the group for screen readers. It can’t be selected. A hairline separates the groups.

components.notFor: A busy button: use Button loading. A wait under a few hundred milliseconds: show nothing.

dos: Wrap one region’s placeholders in one SkeletonGroup, and remove it when the content arrives.
Name what’s loading in the group label: Loading orders, not just Loading.

Use shape="avatar" with the size the real Avatar will have.

Don't put a skeleton on a busy button or control. A busy Button takes loading.
Don't nest one SkeletonGroup inside another. One busy region gets one announcement.
Don't show a skeleton for a wait under a few hundred milliseconds. The flash is worse than the wait.

components.summary: A value or a range picked on a track. Each thumb (the handle you drag) gets its own name. If a range slider shared one name, a screen-reader user (someone using software that reads the page aloud) would get two controls called the same thing.
components.useWhen: A value or range on a track, where the rough position matters and the value is shown.
components.notFor: A precise value with no other way to enter it. Use Input.

props.name: label
props.description: Required. Applied to each thumb. A single thumb gets it as-is, and a range adds "minimum" / "maximum" to the end.

props.name: value
props.description: The value(s), when you control them from outside. One number makes a single slider; two make a range.

props.name: defaultValue
props.description: The starting value(s), when the slider manages them itself (uncontrolled).

props.name: onValueChange
props.description: Fires as the thumb moves.

props.name: min
props.description: The lowest value.

props.name: max
props.description: The highest value.

props.name: step
props.description: The increment for both snapping while dragging and the arrow keys.

props.name: disabled
props.description: Takes it out of the tab order and blocks input.

props.name: formatValue
props.description: One function feeds both the readout and aria-valuetext (the ARIA, or Accessible Rich Internet Applications, attribute a screen reader speaks as the value). So the spoken value and the printed one can’t drift apart, whether the slider is controlled or not.

props.name: showValue
props.description: Shows the current value(s) as a readout.

props.name: className
props.description: Merged with the outer wrapper's classes. Later Tailwind utilities (Tailwind is the CSS framework the system uses) win.

props.name: ref
props.description: Passed through to the Radix Slider root. Radix is the library of accessible building blocks this sits on.

props.name: ...rest
props.description: Every Radix Slider.Root prop except those three, spread onto the root. aria-label and aria-labelledby are left out because the accessible name lives on each thumb, where label puts it. One on the root would do nothing at all, not override anything. children is typed away because this component draws its own Track/Range/Thumbs, and a children prop would be thrown away without any warning.

components.title: Spinner
components.summary: A busy indicator for an indeterminate wait, meaning one with no known end or percentage. It comes in two forms. The ring has a lit arc that grows and slides as it turns. The conveyor is a row of shaded blocks, for a wait that sits inside a line of text.
components.useWhen: A short wait with no known end, inside a control or a line of text.
components.notFor: Progress with a known amount (use Progress), or a wait for a whole page (use Skeleton or LoadingAnimation).

props.name: variant
props.description: The rotating ring, or the block conveyor.

props.name: size
props.description: Ring: a 14px, 20px or 24px (pixel) box. Conveyor: 12px, 14px or 16px glyphs.

props.name: label
props.description: Status text that's hidden on screen. Passing it makes the spinner a live region, an area whose changes screen readers announce on their own.

props.description: Merged with the component's classes. Later Tailwind utilities (the small styling classes this system uses) win.

props.name: ref
props.description: Forwarded to the span element.

props.name: ...rest
props.description: Every native span prop except role, spread onto the span. role is removed from the type instead of being quietly overridden at runtime. api.name: spinnerVariants

dos: Pass label whenever the spinner is the only sign that something's happening.

Leave it decorative inside a control that already announces aria-busy, like Button. aria-busy is an ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications) attribute that tells screen readers a part of the page is still loading.
Name what's loading, not the fact of loading: ‘Loading field kits’, not ‘Loading’.

Don't rely on the rotation alone. It stops when someone has turned on reduced motion in their system settings, so the label carries the meaning.
Don't scale it past lg. A page-level wait needs a skeleton, not a bigger spinner.
Don't bevel it. It's the one round shape in the system. A cut corner on something that rotates would travel around the edge instead of marking one spot.

components.title: Switch
components.summary: An on/off control that acts right away. The thumb's position shows the state, so the meaning still comes through with colour turned off. It takes effect the moment it's flipped.
components.useWhen: An on/off setting that takes effect the moment it's flipped.
components.notFor: A choice in a form that needs a Save. Use Checkbox.

props.description: The checked state, when your code controls it.

props.name: defaultChecked
props.description: The starting state, when the switch manages itself.

props.name: onCheckedChange
props.description: Fires the moment it's flipped.

props.name: disabled
props.description: Takes it out of the tab order and blocks toggling.

props.name: required
props.description: The browser's own form validation.

props.name: name
props.description: The browser's own form field name.

props.name: value
props.description: The browser's own form field value.

props.description: Pair it with a real label through htmlFor.

props.name: className
props.description: Merged with the control's classes. Later Tailwind utilities (the small styling classes this system uses) win.

props.name: ref
props.description: Forwarded to the root button from Radix, the open-source library this switch is built on.

props.name: ...rest
props.description: Every other Radix Switch.Root prop, which means every native button attribute, spread onto the root button. For example aria-describedby, or aria-label when no label element points at it. aria-* attributes are ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications) settings that give screen readers extra information.

keyboard.does: Moves focus to it.
Toggles it.
Toggles it. Radix allows this on a switch, though not on a checkbox.

dos: Use it only when flipping it takes effect right away.
Label it with the thing being switched, not with ‘on’ or ‘off’.
Show the result of the switch near it if the effect isn't visible.
donts: Don't put a switch in a form that needs a Save. Use a Checkbox.
Don't put ‘on’/‘off’ text inside the track. The position already says it, and the text won't fit at 24px.

Don't make the thumb take longer than --duration-base (a timing token) to arrive. A slow switch feels broken. The settle after it arrives only changes its shape, and it ends within --duration-slow, because the state is already readable.
Don't use the squash on anything that isn't a small physical object under the user's finger. On a panel or a page it looks like a wobble.
Don't add a rebound to the thumb. It gives once against the edge and stops. A switch that keeps moving after the state has landed looks unsure.
Don't fill the track with the accent when it's on. Thumb and track changing colour together, mid-flight, is what made the flip look like a twitch.

Held down, it stretches 4px away from the edge it rests on: to the right when off, to the left when on, so it never leaves the track. Flipped, it speeds up across the track, gets a little longer in flight and a little shorter against the far edge, then goes back to its own shape. One give, no bounce.
The control fill, on and off. When it's on, only the border turns to signal.fill. The track doesn't fill with the accent, so the thumb is the one thing that changes colour during a flip.

props.description: The tag text. Required.

components.name: Tooltip
components.title: Tooltip
components.summary: Extra text that shows on hover or focus. It never holds information people can only get there. It doesn't appear on touch screens, it goes away, and someone may never trigger it.
components.useWhen: Extra detail on hover or focus for an element that can take focus, such as an IconButton.
components.notFor: The only label, or the only explanation of an error. Use the label prop or visible text.
requires: One <TooltipProvider> near the root of the app. AppShell and the demo layout each mount one, so a screen doesn't add its own.

props.name: content
props.description: Required. The extra text.

props.name: children
props.description: A single element that can take focus.

props.name: side
props.description: Which side of the trigger the content opens on.

props.name: className
props.description: Merged with the content’s classes. Later Tailwind utilities (the small styling classes this system uses) win.

keyboard.does: Moves focus to the trigger and shows the tooltip. Tabbing on to the next element hides it again.
Dismisses it without moving the pointer. That's required by SC 1.4.13, a success criterion (one numbered rule) in WCAG, the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines.

dos: Use it for the extra detail, never the essential one.
Put it on an element that can take focus. A tooltip on a <div> doesn't reach anyone using a keyboard.
Keep it to one sentence.
Pair it with an IconButton whose label already names the action. Then the tooltip adds detail instead of repeating the name.
donts: Don't put a tooltip on a disabled control. It can't take focus, so nobody can reach the tooltip.
Don't put interactive content inside one. A tooltip is text only and never takes focus.
Don't use it as the only label for an icon button. label does that job.
Don't make it the only place an error is explained.

anatomy.description: Mounted once in AppShell. It sets the 300ms (millisecond) delay, and the 150ms skip window for moving between triggers.
Uses asChild, so no wrapper element is added and the focus order stays as it was.

Portalled, meaning it's rendered in a separate layer of the page, outside its trigger. It enters with motion token M1, is capped at 260px (pixels) wide and has the cut bottom-right corner. It's a single object with its own fill and holds nothing that takes focus, so the cut doesn't need an unclipped wrapper. The trigger, not the panel, is what takes focus.

That's a rule in WCAG 2.2 (the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, the public rulebook for making websites usable by people with disabilities). Its success criterion (SC) 1.4.13 says this kind of content has to stay dismissible (you can close it), hoverable (you can move the pointer onto it) and persistent (it stays until you do).

components.name: Accordion
components.title: Accordion
components.summary: Sections that open and close in place, each under its own heading. You can allow one open at a time or several, and draw them as plain rows split by thin lines or as a panel per section.
components.useWhen: Sections people scan by heading and open one or two of: frequently asked questions (FAQ), grouped settings, long specifications.
components.notFor: Steps in a sequence: use Stepper. Equal views of the same thing: use Tabs.

props.name: type
props.description: Required on the root. single: opening one section closes the other. multiple: any number can be open.

props.name: collapsible
props.description: single mode only. Lets the open section be closed again by its own trigger. You'll want it almost always.

props.name: variant
props.description: plain: thin separator lines, for a long run of questions. boxed: a panel per section, for a few sections that each stand alone.

props.name: value (Root)
props.description: The open section when the page controls it: a string in single mode, an array in multiple mode.

props.name: defaultValue
props.description: The section or sections open at first, when the accordion keeps track itself (uncontrolled). Set on the root.

props.name: onValueChange
props.description: Called when a section opens or closes (on the root). The argument has the same shape as type.

props.name: value (Item)
props.description: Required. The section’s own value.

props.name: disabled (Item)
props.description: The section can't be opened or closed.

props.name: level (Trigger)
props.description: The level of the heading the trigger sits in. Pick one below the heading the accordion appears under.

props.name: forceMount (Content)
props.description: Keeps a closed panel in the page's code (the DOM, the browser's live model of the page), so the browser's find-in-page search can reach its content. It then skips the closing animation.

props.name: className
props.description: Merged with each part’s classes. On AccordionContent it goes on the inner padded box, not the animated clipping box around it.

props.name: ref
props.description: Passed through to the DOM element. Every part has one; the trigger’s is the button.

api.name: AccordionVariant
api.code: export type AccordionVariant = 'plain' | 'boxed'

keyboard.does: Moves between triggers, and into an open section’s content.
Opens or closes the focused section.
Goes to the next or previous trigger, wrapping round at the ends and skipping disabled ones.
Goes to the first or last trigger.

dos: Use it for content people scan by its headings and open one or two of: an FAQ, a group of settings, long specifications.
Write each trigger as the question or the section name, so the closed list reads like a table of contents.
Set collapsible in single mode.
Use boxed for a few sections that each hold controls, and plain for a long list of text answers.
donts: Don't hide the one thing everyone needs inside a closed section. Show it.
Don't use it for steps in a sequence. That's Stepper.
Don't use it to switch between equal views of the same thing. That's Tabs.
Don't nest an accordion inside another accordion's content.

pitfalls.why: Without collapsible, a single-mode accordion can never be fully closed again once a section is open. That surprises people.
Every trigger (the clickable section header) sits inside a heading, h3 (a level-3 heading) by default. Set level so the triggers nest one level below the heading they appear under.

anatomy.description: The root. It holds which sections are open and the variant, and every part below reads both.

One section. plain: a thin line under it. boxed: its own raised panel with the cut corner. The panel is drawn on a backing layer marked aria-hidden (hidden from screen readers), so the item itself is never clipped.
A button inside a heading of the level you choose. It uses the display typeface, has a chevron that turns half a revolution when the section is open, and is underlined on hover.

A region labelled by its trigger, in secondary text. It grows open over the base duration and shrinks shut faster (M7). When someone has asked their device for reduced motion, it snaps open and shut instead.

components.name: Alert
components.title: Alert
components.summary: A message that sits in the page. It shows its tone three ways, as an icon, a word and a colour, so it still reads on a greyscale screen and through a screen reader.
components.useWhen: A message that sits in the page and stays there: a warning about this screen, or a failed load with a retry.
components.notFor: Something that will go away on its own: use Toast.

props.name: tone
props.description: Which colour, icon and word the alert carries.

props.name: title
props.description: Required. Screen readers hear the tone word in front of it.

props.name: children
props.description: The body text.

props.name: live
props.description: Only for an alert added after the page has loaded. It sets the role screen readers use to announce it: hostile and warning get role=alert (announced at once), info and ok get role=status (announced politely).

props.name: onDismiss
props.description: Adds the dismiss button. It runs once the alert has faded and its height has collapsed (M7), not on the click itself, so remove the alert from the page here. With reduced motion it runs straight away.

props.name: dismissLabel
props.description: The name screen readers give the dismiss button.

props.name: action
props.description: For example, a small Button.

props.name: compact
props.description: One line, for a toolbar, table header or card. The body sits inside the title paragraph, so pass plain inline text, not blocks.

props.name: className
props.description: Merged onto the root.

props.name: ref
props.description: Passed through to the root DOM element.

props.name: ...rest
props.description: You can't set role yourself: live decides it.

keyboard.does: Reaches the action, then the dismiss button. The alert itself isn't a stop.

dos: Start the title with what happened, and the body with what to do.
Use live only when the alert appears in response to something the person did.
Name the dismiss button for what it closes when there's more than one alert on a page.
Use compact where a full alert would push the content it describes out of view, and keep the body to a short phrase.
After dismiss, move keyboard focus to the next sensible control. The alert's own dismiss button disappears with it, and focus would otherwise drop back to the top of the page.
donts: Don't use an alert for something that will go away on its own. That's a Toast.
Don't colour the body text in the tone.
Don't put paragraphs or lists inside a compact alert. It's one line of text.
Don't stack more than two alerts. The second one is usually detail for the first.

anatomy.description: A raised surface with a 1px (one pixel) border in the tone's text colour on all four sides. There's no stripe down one side.
Shows the tone without relying on colour. Marked aria-hidden, so screen readers skip it.
'Warning:' before the title. It's hidden on screen and read out by screen readers.
Required.
In secondary text, not in the tone colour.
Optional, usually a small Button.
Optional. A ghost IconButton (an icon-only button with no fill).
One line: a 16px icon, then the title and body as one sentence, then the action and dismiss button. Long text wraps onto a new line instead of being cut off.

components.name: ApprovalRequest
components.title: Approval request
components.summary: A pause before an action that changes something in the real world (a side effect). It shows a preview of exactly what will happen, Approve and Reject buttons, and then a status line that takes keyboard focus.
components.useWhen: An assistant is about to send, change or spend something outside the conversation.
components.notFor: Confirming a destructive action on an ordinary screen: use AlertDialog.
requires: A parent that holds the state and sets it to approved or rejected in onApprove and onReject.

props.name: title
props.description: Required. The action as a question. It also names the section.

props.name: state
props.description: Required. Pending shows the buttons; approved or rejected shows the status line.

props.name: onApprove
props.description: Required. Run the action, then set state to approved.

props.name: onReject
props.description: Required. Set state to rejected. Nothing else happens.

props.name: approveLabel
props.description: The approve button. Say the action, like "Send".

props.name: rejectLabel
props.description: The reject button, like "Don't send".

props.name: approvedLabel
props.description: The status line once approved.

props.name: rejectedLabel
props.description: The status line once rejected.

props.name: className
props.description: Goes on the section.

api.name: ApprovalState
api.code: export type ApprovalState = 'pending' | 'approved' | 'rejected'

keyboard.does: Moves to Approve, then Reject.
Approves or rejects. Focus then moves to the status line that replaces the buttons.

dos: Ask before every action that reaches outside the conversation: a message sent, a record changed, money spent.
Name the buttons for the action ("Send", "Don't send") when the title alone leaves any doubt.
Keep the decided request in the thread. It's the record of what was agreed.
donts: Don't run the action before onApprove. The preview is a promise of what will happen, not a report.
Don't focus the Approve button when the request appears: someone in the middle of typing would approve it with their next Enter.
Don't summarise the preview. Show the email, the change, the amount.

pitfalls.wrong: <ApprovalRequest title="Send the email?" ...>An email to the depot lead.</ApprovalRequest>
pitfalls.right:

pitfalls.why: A person can only approve what they can see. The preview is the content itself, not a summary of it.
Removing it from the page once it's decided drops focus back to the page and wipes the record of what was decided. The component swaps its own buttons for a status line instead.

anatomy.description: Named by the title. Outlined in the signal colour while pending, and a thin line once it's decided.
"Needs your approval" with a shield icon while pending, then "Approval".
The action as a question: "Send this order to Arad depot?"
Exactly what will happen, beside a thin line.
Approve (primary) and Reject (secondary). Neither has focus when the request appears.
Takes the place of the buttons: "Approved by you" or "Rejected". It has tabIndex -1 so it can receive focus from code, and focus moves here when the decision was made here.

components.name: AvatarGroup
components.title: Avatar group
components.summary: Overlapping avatars (small profile pictures) with a “+N” for the rest. It’s a list named by its count, so a screen reader hears “6 members” and then each person. The people behind the “+N” are named in words, never only counted.
components.useWhen: Several people in one place, with a count: a squad, the people on an order, who’s viewing.
components.notFor: Picking people: use MultiSelect.
requires: With overflowTooltip, the root <TooltipProvider>. AppShell and the demo layout each include one.

props.name: people
props.description: Required. Everyone in the group, in the order shown.

props.name: max
props.description: The most avatars drawn. The rest go into the +N chip.

props.name: size
props.description: Passed to every Avatar and to the chip.

props.name: label
props.description: What the group is. The count is added on the end: “Alpha squad, 6 members”.

props.name: overflowTooltip
props.description: Shows the hidden names in a Tooltip on the chip and lets the chip take keyboard focus.

props.name: className
props.description: Merged with the list classes. Later Tailwind utility classes win.

props.name: ref
props.description: Passed through to the list.

props.name: ...rest
props.description: Every standard ul prop except children (the people are the content) and aria-label (label builds it, with the count).

props.name: name (AvatarGroupPerson)
props.description: Required. Passed to Avatar.

props.name: src (AvatarGroupPerson)
props.description: Optional image, passed to Avatar.

props.name: status (AvatarGroupPerson)
props.description: Optional presence (whether they’re online), passed to Avatar, which includes it in the name screen readers hear.

api.name: AvatarGroupPerson
api.code: export type AvatarGroupPerson = { name: string; src?: string; status?: AvatarStatus }

keyboard.does: With overflowTooltip, focuses the +N chip and opens the tooltip. Otherwise nothing in the group can take focus.

dos: Give it a label that says who the people are: a squad, the people on an order, who’s viewing.
Keep max at four or fewer in dense rows. The chip covers the rest.
Put the full list somewhere people can reach (a dialog, a roster page) when they need to act on it.
donts: Don't use it as a control. To pick people, use MultiSelect. To open the list, put a Button next to it.
Don't set overflowTooltip on every row of a long table, because each chip becomes a Tab stop.
Don't pass aria-label. The label plus the count is the name.

pitfalls.why: A hand-built stack has no count, no thin outline between the faces, and no words for the people a +N leaves out.

Shaped like an avatar, in monospaced text in text.secondary. The “+2” is aria-hidden (screen readers skip it), and hidden text reading “and 2 more: …” names the people it stands for.
Optional. Shows the hidden names on hover and on keyboard focus. The chip then becomes a Tab stop, with its focus ring drawn on an outer box that isn’t clipped.

components.name: Breadcrumbs
components.title: Breadcrumbs
components.summary: Shows where this page sits among the pages above it. The last level is the current page, shown as text. Every level above it is a link.
components.useWhen: Showing where a page sits in a hierarchy more than one level deep.
components.notFor: Steps in a sequence: use Stepper.

props.name: items
props.description: { label, href? }. A level with no href shows as plain text.

props.name: maxItems
props.description: Collapse the trail when it has more levels than this. It never goes below 3.

props.name: label
props.description: The name of the nav landmark.

props.name: className

api.name: Crumb

api.name: collapseCrumbs

components.name: Card
components.title: Card
components.summary: A surface that groups related content. It gets the crosshair corners, the visual mark this system uses for a frame around several things. It never gets the cut corner, because cards hold buttons.
components.useWhen: Grouping related content on one surface, or one item in a grid whose whole surface is one link.
components.notFor: A card inside another card: cards don't nest.

props.name: as
props.description: article for an item that stands on its own, section for a group inside a page, div for neither.

props.name: interactive
props.description: Says the whole card is one click target, through a link or button stretched over it. Adds the hover and focus border and a 4px lift. It adds no role and no Tab stop: the link inside is still the control.

props.name: level (CardTitle)
props.description: The heading level, set on CardTitle only. Card itself takes no level. The page decides its own outline.

props.name: src (CardMedia)
props.description: The picture, drawn with object-cover (it fills the box and crops the overflow) and loaded lazily (only when it's about to scroll into view). Leave it out to show CardMedia's children instead, such as a placeholder.

props.name: alt (CardMedia)
props.description: The alt text screen readers read for the picture. Empty by default: the picture is decorative because the card title already names it. Write real text only when the picture says something the title doesn't.

props.name: aspect (CardMedia)
props.description: The shape of the box the picture is cropped to.

props.name: className
props.description: Merged onto any part.

props.name: ...rest
props.description: Standard HTML attributes on every part, except aria-labelledby on Card: the Card points that at its CardTitle itself, and the types won't accept one passed in. Give CardTitle an id only if something else needs it.

props.name: ref
props.description: Passed through to the Card root DOM element.

api.name: cardLinkClass

keyboard.does: Moves through the card's own buttons and links. The card itself isn't a stop, interactive or not. Focus on anything inside an interactive card lights its border and lifts it 4px.

dos: Put actions in CardFooter when the card ends in an action bar. It's a right-aligned row with the gap between buttons already set and the primary last. A fullWidth button fills it.
Put actions in CardActions, inside CardBody, when the button belongs to the text above it and there should be no bar. Primary first, then the secondary.
Wherever a card has a primary button, put a secondary or ghost button beside it (Details, Cancel), unless the card really has only one action.
Give every card a title, even a short one. It names the card for screen readers.
Put CardMedia first in the card, and give a row of cards the same aspect, so the titles line up.
Give every card in a row the same parts, so they line up.
Use section for a group inside a page and article for an item that stands on its own.
Set interactive on a card whose whole surface is one link, and only on those: a product, a category tile.
Make the click target a real link stretched over the card from its title, so the name, the focus ring and middle-click all belong to the link.
donts: Don't make the whole card a link by wrapping it in an a element. That puts clickable things inside a clickable thing. Stretch the title's link over the card and set interactive.
Don't set interactive on a card that only holds a button or a link somewhere inside it. The lit border promises that a click anywhere does something.
Don't add your own hover border, lift or glow to a card. There's one prop and one treatment, so every clickable card responds the same way.
Don't clip an interactive card: it lifts 4px and its crosshair arms reach 5px outside it. Carousel leaves that room by itself.
Don't put CardActions and CardFooter in the same card. Two places to act, with opposite alignment and order, read as two different decisions.
Don't right-align CardActions or put the primary last in it. The two parts differ on purpose: the bar is on the right with the primary last, the inline row is on the left with the primary first.
Don't pad around a picture to fake CardMedia, or wrap it in CardBody. The picture runs edge to edge, so it goes directly in the Card.
Don't bevel a card.
Don't nest cards.

pitfalls.why: The panel sets its own border outside any CSS cascade layer, so a border utility class never wins. To highlight or select a card, set the border inline, using a token (one of the system's named design values).

anatomy.description: The root. An article element by default, named by its title. Uses the .panel and .crosshair classes.

Only with interactive. On hover, and while anything inside has keyboard focus, the thin border turns accent.signal.fill and the whole card slides up 4px (four pixels). It slides back down when the pointer leaves or focus moves on. It's a CSS transform, so nothing around it moves. When someone has turned on reduced motion (prefers-reduced-motion), the border still changes but the card doesn't move.

A picture across the full width of the card, flush with the top and side edges inside the border, cropped to an aspect ratio. It's the first child, before CardHeader or CardBody. Without a src, its children fill the box instead (a placeholder).
Groups the title and description.
A heading at whatever level the page needs, 3 by default.
A short secondary line under the title.
Grows to fill the space, so the footers in a row of cards line up.
The action bar: right-aligned, with the primary button last (rightmost), above a thin line that runs edge to edge. It's where a task ends, the same position as DialogFooter.

Actions inside the content, placed in CardBody after the text. A row that wraps, left-aligned, primary first and secondary after it, with no line and no bar. It's on the left because people read a body down its left edge, so the button stays next to the text it acts on at any card width.

components.name: ChatMessage
components.title: Chat message
components.summary: One turn in a conversation with an assistant: the person's words in a bubble, the reply at full width, or a centred system line. While a reply is still streaming in, it sets aria-busy (an ARIA, Accessible Rich Internet Applications, attribute that tells screen readers the content isn't finished) and shows a caret that doesn't blink.
components.useWhen: Each turn inside a ChatThread.
components.notFor: Comments or an activity history between people: use Timeline.
requires: A ChatThread around it. Outside one, a message still shows, but nothing announces it when it finishes.

props.name: role
props.description: Required. Who's speaking. system is a quiet, centred status line.

props.name: author
props.description: Required. "You", "Assistant". It names the message.

props.name: time
props.description: The date and time in ISO format (the international standard way of writing them), for <time dateTime>.

props.name: timeLabel
props.description: The time as shown on screen: "09:40".

props.name: streaming
props.description: The text is still arriving: sets aria-busy and shows a caret. Inside a ChatThread, the finished text is announced once, when this turns false.

props.name: actions
props.description: Small buttons under an assistant message. They aren't shown on a user message.

props.name: className
props.description: Goes on the article.

api.name: ChatMessageRole
api.code: export type ChatMessageRole = 'user' | 'assistant' | 'system'

keyboard.does: Moves to the controls inside the message: a ToolCall's details, an approval's buttons, the actions.

dos: Keep streaming true until the last piece of text has arrived, then set it to false once.
Put tool calls and approvals in the assistant message where they happened, in order with its text.
Use a system line for events in the conversation itself: stopped, retried, context cleared.
Give every message an author, including a system line ("Status"). It names the article.
donts: Don't animate the text in yourself. useStreamedText or your stream supplies it, and the thread handles announcing it.
Don't put actions on the person's own message. Editing a sent message is a different flow.
Don't colour the assistant's text. The bubble, the alignment and the author line already tell the roles apart.

pitfalls.why: streaming sets aria-busy, draws a caret that doesn't blink, and tells the thread to announce the text once, when it's finished. A hand-made blinking caret flashes for the whole stream.

anatomy.description: Named by the author line, so a screen reader hears who's speaking first. Has aria-busy while streaming.
The author as a label in monospaced type, then the time in a <time dateTime> element.
The person's words on surface.sunken, aligned right, at most 85% of the width.
Full width, with no bubble: text, paragraphs, and ToolCall and ApprovalRequest blocks stacked in a column.
A solid block in the signal colour after the last paragraph while streaming, drawn with the CSS ::after rule. It never blinks.
Small buttons under an assistant message: Copy, Retry.
A centred label in monospaced type between two thin lines: "Assistant stopped". Its author is there for screen readers only.
