components.name: DescriptionList
components.title: Description list
components.summary: Pairs of a term and its value, all about one thing, in one to three columns. The columns drop away as the space they get narrows. It's a real dl (the HTML description list element): a label in a monospaced font over each value, and a thin line above each pair.
components.useWhen: The fixed fields of one record: serial, firmware, owner, dates.
components.notFor: Many records: use DataTable; one headline number: use Stat.

props.name: items
props.description: Required. The pairs, in the order people read them.

props.name: columns
props.description: How many columns at full width. It drops to one when the container is narrower than 28rem.

props.name: className
props.description: On the container.

props.name: ref
props.description: Forwarded to the container.

props.name: term (DescriptionListItem)
props.description: Required. The field name: "Serial".

props.name: description (DescriptionListItem)
props.description: Required. Its value.

api.name: DescriptionListItem

keyboard.does: Moves to any link or button inside a description.

dos: Order pairs the way someone reads the record: identity first, then state, then dates.
Say "None" or "Not set" for an empty value rather than leaving the description blank.
Use two or three columns only for short values; long text reads better in one.
donts: Don't use it for a list of records. That's what DataTable is for.
Don't put a form field in a description. A record people can edit is a form.
Don't repeat a term inside one list.

anatomy.description: A div with @container (a container query), so the columns follow the width of this box, not of the screen.
A dl laid out as a grid: one column, two from 28rem wide, three from 42rem (as far as columns allows). A rem is the base text size, usually 16 pixels.
A div holding one dt (the term) and one dd (its value), with a thin line above.
The dt, styled as a label: monospaced, uppercase, 11px (pixels).
The dd, in body text. It holds text, a Badge or a Link.

components.name: DropdownMenu
components.title: Dropdown menu
components.summary: A short list of actions behind a button. It uses the same background as Select, so the system's two pop-ups look like one family. The highlighted item gets a fill, as it does everywhere else.
components.useWhen: A short list of actions, under about eight, behind a button.
components.notFor: Picking a value for a form: use Select.

props.name: open (Root)
props.description: Whether the menu is open, when the page keeps track of it (controlled).

props.name: defaultOpen (Root)
props.description: Whether it starts open, when the menu keeps track itself (uncontrolled).

props.name: onOpenChange (Root)
props.description: Called when the menu opens or closes.

props.name: modal (Root)
props.description: While open, keyboard focus stays inside the menu and the page behind can't scroll.

props.name: align (Content)
props.description: Alignment against the trigger.

props.name: side (Content)
props.description: Preferred side of the trigger.

props.name: sideOffset (Content)
props.description: Gap between trigger and content, in pixels.

props.name: onSelect (Item)
props.description: Called when the item is chosen.

props.name: disabled (Item)
props.description: The item can't be chosen, and typing letters (typeahead) skips it.

props.name: tone (Item)
props.description: Use hostile for a destructive action: hostile-coloured text at rest, the hostile fill with ink text when highlighted.

props.name: icon (Item)
props.description: A small icon before the text, hidden from screen readers (aria-hidden).

props.name: shortcut (Item)
props.description: Shown on the right and passed to screen readers as aria-keyshortcuts. It only displays the key: the menu never makes the key work.

props.name: checked (Checkbox item)
props.description: Whether the tick shows.

props.name: onCheckedChange (Checkbox item)
props.description: Called when the checkbox item is toggled.

props.name: value (RadioGroup)
props.description: The checked radio item.

props.name: onValueChange (RadioGroup)
props.description: Called with the chosen radio item value.

props.name: value (RadioItem)
props.description: This radio item's own value.

props.name: icon (SubTrigger)
props.description: A small icon before the text, hidden from screen readers, as on Item.

props.name: open / defaultOpen / onOpenChange (Sub)
props.description: Whether the submenu is open, tracked by the page (controlled) or by the submenu (uncontrolled). You'll usually leave these alone.

props.name: alignOffset (SubContent)
props.description: Shifts the submenu so its first row lines up with its trigger.

props.name: className
props.description: Extra CSS classes, merged with the part's own. When two Tailwind classes clash, the later one wins. Every part takes it.

props.name: ref
props.description: Passed through to the rendered element (the DOM node). On Content, Item, Checkbox item, Radio item, Sub trigger and Sub content.

keyboard.does: On the trigger: opens, highlighting the first item.
Moves the highlight.
Jumps to the first or last item.
Runs the highlighted item.
Closes the menu and puts focus back on the trigger.
On a sub trigger: opens the submenu, highlighting its first item.
In a submenu: closes it, and you're back on its trigger.
Typeahead: jumps to the next item that starts with the letters you type.

dos: Keep menus under about eight items.
Put the destructive item last, after a separator, with the hostile tone.
Name an icon-only trigger for what the menu holds: 'Manifest actions', not 'More'.
Use a radio group for a setting the menu shows the current value of: sort order, density.
Name a sub trigger for what it holds: 'Move to', 'Export as'.
donts: Don't use a menu to pick a value for a form. That's what Select is for.
Don't put a submenu inside a submenu. One level at most.
Don't use radio items to run actions. A radio item sets a value, and the menu keeps showing it.
Don't make every item hostile to add weight. Hostile means it destroys something.

anatomy.description: A Button or IconButton, passed in through asChild. Radix (the library underneath) adds aria-haspopup and aria-expanded. These are ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications) attributes that tell screen readers the button opens a menu and whether it's open.

Rendered in a portal, at the end of the page, so nothing clips it. Sunken surface, a strong thin border, crosshair corners. M7: it slides down out of the trigger to open and back up into it to close (the other way round when it opens above).
36px (pixels) tall. When highlighted: the signal fill with ink-coloured text.
For a destructive action. Hostile-coloured text at rest, and the hostile fill with ink text when highlighted.
Shows a tick when on. Screen readers get it as a menuitemcheckbox with aria-checked.

Uses text.secondary, so it reads as a heading over the items. It doesn't use text.label: on this background (surface.sunken) that token fails SC 1.4.3, the contrast rule in WCAG (the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines).
A thin line.
One choice in a RadioGroup. Screen readers get it as a menuitemradio with aria-checked. Its mark is a small filled square, never a dot.
An item with a chevron that opens a submenu. While the highlight is inside the submenu, the sub trigger keeps a 1px strong line just inside its edge.
The submenu: the same surface and M7 slide as Content, aligned so its first row sits level with its trigger.
Text on the right that screen readers skip (aria-hidden), plus aria-keyshortcuts on the item so they announce it once. It only displays the key: the page has to make the key work.

components.name: EmptyState
components.title: Empty state
components.summary: What a list, a table or a page region shows when it has nothing in it: an icon, a title that names what is empty, a sentence on why, and the action that fills it.
components.useWhen: A list, table or region with nothing in it, along with the action that fills it.
components.notFor: A list that's still loading: use Skeleton or Spinner. A failed load: use Alert in the hostile tone.

props.name: title
props.description: Required. What is empty, said plainly: “No orders yet”.

props.name: level
props.description: Required, with no default. The heading level the page's outline of headings needs at this point.

props.name: description
props.description: One or two sentences: why it's empty, or what fills it.

props.name: icon
props.description: A lucide icon element. The component sizes it and wraps it in a tile that screen readers skip (aria-hidden).

props.name: actions
props.description: One or two Buttons. The component lays out the row and its gap.

props.name: size
props.description: md for a page region. sm inside a table, a card or a panel.

props.name: framed
props.description: The dashed frame. Turn it off where the container already draws an edge.

props.name: className
props.description: Extra CSS classes, merged onto the outer element. When two Tailwind classes clash, the later one wins.

props.name: ref
props.description: Passed through to the outer element.

props.name: ...rest
props.description: Any other div attribute, put on the outer element. role="status" goes here when nothing else on the page tells screen readers that the list has emptied.

keyboard.does: Moves through the actions, if there are any. The empty state itself never takes keyboard focus.

dos: Name what is empty in the title (“No orders yet”), not the state (“Empty”).
Say in the description what fills it, or why a filter emptied it.
Offer the action that fixes it: “Clear filters” after a filter, “Browse replicas” on an empty wishlist.
Use size="sm" and framed={false} inside a table, a card or a panel.
donts: Don’t use it for a list that’s still loading. Nothing has been found yet, so show a spinner or a skeleton.
Don’t use it for an error. A failed load is an Alert in the hostile tone, with a retry.
Don’t put more than two actions in it. A third belongs on the page, not in the empty region.
Don’t add role="status" when a count on the page already announces the change. A screen reader user would hear it twice.

pitfalls.why: The level is required, because only the page knows what the empty region is: a whole page (an h2, a level-2 heading, under the h1), a section (h3) or a card (h4).
The card already draws an edge, so a dashed frame inside it makes a second one. And the md (medium) padding is sized for a page region.

anatomy.description: A dashed edge in border.hairline-strong. It's the one border in the system that reads as an empty slot instead of a surface. Optional, through framed.
Optional. A square on surface.sunken with a thin edge, holding a lucide icon in text.secondary. Screen readers skip it (aria-hidden), because the title already says what the icon would.
A heading element, h2 to h4. Oxanium, semibold, 18px (pixels) at md size and 16px at sm (small), in text.primary.
Optional. 14px body text in text.secondary, with lines no longer than 48 characters.
Optional. One or two Buttons, centred, in a row that wraps onto a new line with a 12px gap.

components.name: FormField
components.title: FormField
components.summary: The label, help text and error text for one form control. They're connected so a screen reader reads all three, in that order, when the control gets focus. The atoms (the smallest components) never label themselves. This is where it happens.
components.useWhen: The label, help and error for an Input, Textarea, Select, MultiSelect or QuantityStepper.
components.notFor: Search or RatingInput, which name themselves. Switch, Checkbox and Radio take an id and a label with htmlFor instead.

props.name: label
props.description: The field label. Required.

props.name: help
props.description: Instruction text, read out before any error.

props.name: error
props.description: Sets invalid on the control and adds the error line.

props.name: required
props.description: Adds the asterisk (hidden from screen readers) and the built-in required attribute on the control. That attribute is what assistive technology actually announces.

props.name: children
props.description: Exactly one control: Input, Textarea, Select or QuantityStepper. A label set on a Select or QuantityStepper child is replaced by the FormField label.

props.name: className
props.description: Extra CSS classes, merged with the outer element's own. When two Tailwind classes clash, the later one wins.

props.name: ref
props.description: Passed through to the outer element.

props.name: errors (ErrorSummary)
props.description: What stopped the form from submitting, in the order of the fields. Each entry links to its field and moves focus there. An empty list shows nothing.

props.name: title (ErrorSummary)
props.description: The heading. It's what a screen reader reads first when the form moves focus to the summary.

props.name: headingLevel (ErrorSummary)
props.description: The heading level, so the summary fits the outline of headings on its page.

props.name: className (ErrorSummary)
props.description: Extra CSS classes, merged with the outer element's own. When two Tailwind classes clash, the later one wins.

props.name: ref (ErrorSummary)
props.description: The summary itself. A form moves focus to it after a submit that failed.

api.name: FormError

keyboard.does: Moves to the control. FormField adds no keyboard stops of its own.

dos: Pass an id to the control when something else has to point at it (an ErrorSummary entry, a link). FormField keeps an id you give it and only makes one up when you don't.
Keep help text to the one thing people get wrong.
Write the error as what to do next: 'Use four to eight letters', not 'Invalid'.
Check the value when someone leaves the field (on blur) or submits, not on every keystroke.
Wrap a Select or a QuantityStepper: FormField hands it the id, the description, the invalid state and its own label.
donts: Don't wrap Search or RatingInput. Each is named by its own label and takes no help or error text.
Don't hide the help text when an error appears. That's when people need the instruction most.
Don't use placeholder text as the label. It disappears the moment someone types.
Don't show a field error on a raised panel. Field errors sit on surface.base.

anatomy.description: A real label element that points at the control's id. Monospaced, 11px (pixels), uppercase.
A signal-orange asterisk that screen readers skip (aria-hidden). Assistive technology, such as screen readers, announces the built-in HTML required attribute instead.

The single child, copied with id, aria-describedby, invalid and required added. aria-describedby is an ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications) attribute that links the control to its help and error text.
Optional. Read out first.
Optional. Read out after the help, with an icon so the error isn't shown by colour alone. It isn't a live region, so it isn't announced the moment it appears.

components.name: ListItem
components.title: List item
components.summary: One row of a list: something at the start (a picture or icon), a title and description, extra details on the right, and actions at the end. A row that goes somewhere is one real link or button stretched over the whole row. Its actions sit beside it, never inside it.
components.useWhen: A row people scan in a List: media, a title, meta and one or two actions.
components.notFor: Data in a table that people compare across columns: use DataTable.
requires: A <List> around the rows (a ul with role="list"), or as="div" on a row that stands alone.

props.name: title
props.description: Required. The main line, and the name screen readers give the row’s link or button.

props.name: description
props.description: A second line under the title, in secondary text.

props.name: media
props.description: Something at the start of the row: an Avatar, an icon (hidden from screen readers with aria-hidden), a thumbnail.

props.name: meta
props.description: Right-aligned monospaced text: a time, a price, a count.

props.name: actions
props.description: Controls at the end. Each one can still be focused and clicked on its own.

props.name: href
props.description: Makes the row one link to this address, named by the title.

props.name: renderLink
props.description: Draws the row link when href is set. Pass your router's link here. It has to pass className through.

props.name: onActivate
props.description: Makes the row one button, named by the title. Ignored when href is set.

props.name: as
props.description: li inside a List. div for a row on its own.

props.name: dividers (List)
props.description: A thin line between rows.

props.name: className
props.description: Extra CSS classes, merged with the outer element's own classes on List or ListItem.

props.name: ref
props.description: Passed through to the ul (List) or the row element (ListItem).

keyboard.does: Moves to the row’s link or button, then to each of its actions, then to the next row.
Follows the row’s link, or presses its button.
Presses the row’s button (a link row ignores Space, like any link).

dos: Put rows in a List, and give the List an aria-label (a name only screen readers hear) when no heading names it.
Use href when the row opens a page, and onActivate when it does something right there.
Keep actions to one or two. Put the rest in a DropdownMenu.
When an action repeats on every row, name it after its row ("Sign out of Chrome on Windows"), with aria-label or the IconButton label.
donts: Don't make a row clickable with onClick on the row. Use href or onActivate.

components.title: Page header
components.summary: The top of a screen. It holds the page’s one h1 (the main, level-1 heading), and can add an eyebrow, a description, a breadcrumb trail and the page’s own actions at the far edge.

components.notFor: A section inside a page: use SectionHeading.

props.description: Required. The page’s name, shown as its h1.

props.name: eyebrow

props.name: description

props.name: actions

props.name: breadcrumbs

props.name: id
props.description: Goes on the h1, not the wrapper, so main can point aria-labelledby at it. That ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications) attribute lets the main area take its name from the heading.

props.name: level
props.description: Use 2 only for a page-style header inside a page that already has its h1 (a pane, a tab panel). It looks the same either way.

Put the page’s primary action last in the actions row, so it lands at the far edge.

Don’t put the page’s filters or tabs in the actions slot. They belong to the content under it.
Don’t repeat the title in the eyebrow. The eyebrow names where the page sits, and the title names the page.

components.title: Pagination

components.useWhen: Moving through a long list or table one page at a time.

props.description: The name of the nav landmark (a region screen readers can jump to).

api.name: paginationRange
api.code:
/** Pure. 1-based. Always includes page 1, the last page, the current page and `siblings` pages
 *  either side of it. A gap stands for two or more hidden pages; a single hidden page is shown
 *  instead, because a gap that hides one number costs the same space as the number. */
export function paginationRange(page: number, pageCount: number, siblings = 1): (number | 'gap')[]

Goes to that page.
In the Go to page field, jumps to the page you typed.

After a change, move focus to the top of the new page of results.
Keep siblings at 1 on narrow layouts.
Under a data table, pass totalItems and pageSize. The footer then says what's on view, so you don't need a separate line of text.
Use variant 'compact' where space is tight, such as a card or a phone layout.

Don't disable the current page; Tab would skip it.
Don't use pagination for steps in a form.
Don't use variant 'select' for hundreds of pages. A list that long needs showJump instead.
Don't round the buttons into circles or pills; the square and the cut corner are this system's shape.

It stays a real stop when you press Tab, so keyboard focus never drops to the page body when one stops working.

api.name: gridMax
api.code:
/** The step grid's own last rung at or below `max` -- the real upper bound the control can reach.
 *  `max` itself may not be a step away from `min` (min 0, max 99, step 5: the grid is 0, 5, ...,
 *  95, and 99 is never a rung on it), so this is what `aria-valuemax`, the Increase button's
 *  disabled state, the focus-on-bound check and End all need instead of `max` directly -- a control
 *  that can never reach the value it announces as its maximum is worse than one that announces a
 *  lower, reachable one. */
export function gridMax(min: number, max: number, step = 1): number

api.name: clampQuantity
api.code:
/**
 * Pure. Parses, snaps to the step grid measured from min, then clamps into `[min, gridMax(min,
 * max, step)]`. Unparseable input returns `min`.
 *
 * `min > max` is the caller's error, not this function's to reject: the formula has no branch that
 * assumes `min <= max`, so it still returns a number rather than throwing -- just not a meaningful
 * one for an inverted range. Callers are expected to pass a sane range.
 */
export function clampQuantity(raw: string | number, min: number, max: number, step = 1): number

Ten steps.
Jumps to the minimum or maximum.
Confirms what you typed.
Leaves the field and confirms what you typed. Tab doesn't stop on the buttons.

Name the field after the item: 'Speed loader quantity'.
Show the line total beside it, updating as the value changes.
donts: Don't use it for values that aren't whole numbers; that's an Input.
Don't use it for a range of hundreds; that's a Slider or an Input.
Don't pull the value back inside the limits while someone's still typing.

A toast follows the innermost open overlay (a dialog or panel on top of the page). components.name: AlertDialog
components.title: Alert dialog
components.summary: Asks for confirmation before something with real consequences. It shows a question, says what will happen, and offers Cancel and the action. Screen readers announce it as an alert, a click outside won't dismiss it, and focus starts on Cancel. If the action returns a promise (a value that finishes later, such as a server call), the dialog stays open and shows it's busy until that work is done.
components.useWhen: Confirming an action that matters and can't be undone, such as a delete.
components.notFor: Something that can be undone: just do it and offer Undo in a Toast. A form or a task: use Dialog.

props.name: open (AlertDialog)
props.description: Whether it is open, when your code controls that (controlled mode).

props.name: defaultOpen (AlertDialog)
props.description: Whether it starts open, when the component tracks its own state (uncontrolled mode).

props.name: onOpenChange (AlertDialog)
props.description: Called on every open and close. It isn't called when someone tries to close it while the action is busy.

props.name: asChild (Trigger)
props.description: Uses its single child as the trigger instead of adding its own button. Pass a Button.

props.name: ref (Trigger)
props.description: The trigger button.

props.name: title (Content)
props.description: Required. The question, and the name screen readers say.

props.name: description (Content)
props.description: Required. What confirming does. Screen readers read it as the accessible description.

props.name: size (Content)
props.description: Maximum width: 24rem or 32rem (rem is a unit based on the root text size, usually 16 pixels).

props.name: className (Content)
props.description: Added to the panel classes. Where two Tailwind utility classes clash, the later one wins.

props.name: ref (Content)
props.description: The element with the role alertdialog.

props.name: onPointerDownOutside / onInteractOutside (Content)
props.description: Not available: a click outside never dismisses an alert dialog.

props.name: className (Footer)
props.description: Added to the button row classes.

props.name: children (Cancel)
props.description: The label. Name what the person keeps, for example Keep editing.

props.name: ref (Cancel)
props.description: The Cancel button, which gets focus when the dialog opens.

props.name: tone (Action)
props.description: hostile (the danger button) for something that can't be undone. default (the primary button) for a confirm that's safe but still matters.

props.name: onClick (Action)
props.description: Runs on confirm, then closes the dialog. If it returns a promise, the dialog stays open and busy until the promise settles: success closes it, failure keeps it open. Calling event.preventDefault() also keeps it open.

props.name: loading (Action)
props.description: Marks it busy from outside, for work you track yourself. It holds the dialog open the same way a pending promise does.

props.name: loadingLabel (Action)
props.description: Text you can't see that screen readers announce while it's busy.

props.name: ref (Action)
props.description: The action button.

keyboard.does: Moves between Cancel, the action and any field, looping around inside the dialog.
Presses the focused button. Focus starts on Cancel, so an accidental Enter cancels.
Cancels and sends focus back to whatever opened it. It waits while the action is busy.

dos: Write the title as the question, with the thing it's about: 'Delete Brasov north?', not 'Are you sure?'.
Say in the description exactly what will be lost or changed, with numbers where you have them.
Label the action with the verb and the thing: 'Delete depot', never 'OK' or 'Yes'.
Return the promise from onClick for anything that calls a server.
For something very costly, add a field asking for the name, and disable the action until it matches (see the last example).
donts: Don't use it for something that can be undone. Do the thing and offer Undo in a toast.
Don't use it for a form or a task. That's a Dialog.
Don't add a close button or close it on a click outside. The only choices are Cancel or the action.
Don't open one from a dropdown menu item. The item is gone by the time the dialog closes, so focus has nowhere to go back to.

pitfalls.right:
<AlertDialog>
  <AlertDialogContent title="Delete depot?" description="Its open manifests move to the unassigned queue.">
    <AlertDialogFooter>
      <AlertDialogCancel />
      <AlertDialogAction onClick={remove}>Delete depot</AlertDialogAction>
    </AlertDialogFooter>
  </AlertDialogContent>
</AlertDialog>
pitfalls.why: Dialog has the role dialog (the label screen readers use to describe it), closes when someone clicks the scrim behind it, and focuses the first control. A destructive confirm needs the role alertdialog, no dismissal from outside, and focus on Cancel. AlertDialog does all three.
Return the promise. The action goes busy, Cancel and Escape wait, and the dialog closes when the work succeeds or stays open when it fails. You don't need any state of your own.

pitfalls.wrong:
<AlertDialogAction onClick={() => remove()}>Delete</AlertDialogAction>
// remove() rejects, and nothing tells the person
pitfalls.right:
<AlertDialogAction onClick={() => remove().catch(error => {
  toast({ tone: 'hostile', title: 'Not deleted', description: error.message })
  throw error
})}>Delete</AlertDialogAction>
pitfalls.why: When the promise fails, the dialog stays open but shows nothing on its own. Report the failure, then throw the error again so the dialog stays open for a retry or a Cancel.

anatomy.description: The dimmed layer over the page, coloured surface.scrim. The page under it is inert (it can't be clicked or focused) and hidden from screen readers. Unlike Dialog, clicking it does nothing: the person has to choose.
The same panel as Dialog: surface.base, a strong hairline border, the corner crosshair and the M7 motion for opening and closing. Its role is alertdialog.
Required. The question. It's an h2 (a second-level heading) and the dialog's accessible name, the name screen readers say for it.
Required. What confirming does. Screen readers announce it with the title.
Optional. A list of what will be lost, or a field to type a name into.
Cancel first, then the action. There's no close button.

components.name: AuthForm
components.title: Auth form
components.summary: One form with four modes: sign in, create an account, reset a password, or enter a two-step code. It's built so password managers, pasting and keyboards all just work.
components.useWhen: Sign in, create an account, reset a password or enter a two-step code.
components.notFor: A newsletter sign-up: use NewsletterForm. Any other form: build it from FormField controls.

props.name: mode
props.description: Required. Which form shows.

props.name: onSubmit
props.type: (values: AuthValues, mode: AuthMode) => void | AuthErrors | Promise<void | AuthErrors>
props.description: Required. Runs once every field passes its checks. Resolve with errors keyed by field name to show them. If it rejects, a general alert for the whole form appears, so the failure isn't lost.

props.name: onModeChange
props.description: Offers the other modes and reports when someone switches.

props.name: headingLevel
props.description: Match the page's heading outline. The error summary sits one level below. The exception is 4, the lowest heading this system uses: there the summary stays an h4 (a level-4 heading) too.

props.name: className
props.description: Merged with the root classes. Later Tailwind utilities win.

props.name: ref
props.description: The form.

api.name: AuthMode
api.code: export type AuthMode = 'sign-in' | 'create-account' | 'reset-password' | 'verify-code'

api.name: AuthField
api.code: export type AuthField = 'name' | 'email' | 'password' | 'code'

api.name: AuthValues
api.code: export type AuthValues = Record<AuthField, string>

api.name: AuthErrors
api.code: export type AuthErrors = FieldErrors<AuthField>

keyboard.does: Moves through the fields (the password field, then its Show password button), the submit button and the mode links.
In a field, submits. On an error summary entry or a mode link, activates it.
On Show password, toggles it. On a mode link, activates it.

dos: Let password managers work. Every field has its autocomplete token, and pasting is never blocked.
Resolve onSubmit with errors keyed by field (a wrong password, say), so they show in the summary and at the field.
Expect a rejected onSubmit to show up as its own alert instead of failing silently. There's no field to attach it to.
Keep the reset confirmation neutral. It never says whether an account exists.
donts: Don't add a CAPTCHA, a puzzle or a copy-paste block. Signing in mustn't test memory or copying by hand (WCAG success criterion 3.3.8; WCAG is the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, the public rulebook for usable websites).
Don't disable the submit button while fields are empty. The error summary says what's missing.
Don't validate on every keystroke.

Don't count on an error keyed to a field the current mode doesn't show (name while signing in, for example) landing where you'd expect. It's moved onto email, and a console.warn that only shows in development names it. Key it to a field the mode actually shows instead.

anatomy.description: Names the form. Focus (the place your keyboard typing goes) moves here after a mode switch.

Shows up when a submit fails and takes focus. Each entry jumps to its field. It waits for a real submit attempt: leaving a field (a blur) never brings it up, so it can't shove aside a field someone's about to click.
A FormField around each Input, with its help and error text connected to it.

An icon button inside the password field that shows the typed text. It uses Input's revealable option, reports on or off through aria-pressed (ARIA, Accessible Rich Internet Applications, is a set of attributes that tell screen readers what a control is doing), and keeps the same name either way. The text hides again on submit and on a mode switch.
A Button that stays focusable and shows it's busy while the caller works.
A status line that's always on the page. Reset mode uses it.
An alert that's always present and gets its text when onSubmit rejects (the visible copy only appears then). It clears on the next submit and on a mode switch.

Shown when onModeChange is given: forgot password, create an account, back to sign in. They're buttons, since they change the form in place, but they look exactly like Link: signal text, an underline that thickens on hover, a pointer cursor and a focus ring.

components.name: Carousel
components.title: Carousel
components.summary: A row of items that scrolls sideways. The browser does the scrolling, and Previous and Next move it a page at a time. Nothing ever moves on its own.
components.useWhen: A sideways preview of more items than fit, with a link to the full list nearby.
components.notFor: A few items that fit: use a grid. And it's not for the only copy of anything.

props.name: label
props.description: Required. The region's accessible name (the name a screen reader announces), for example "Offers". Leaving it out is a compile error.

props.name: children
props.description: Each child becomes one list item and keeps its own key.

props.name: itemWidth
props.description: Any CSS length. A percentage is a share of the track's width. Keep it under the full width, so the edge of the next item shows.

props.name: gutter
props.description: The space between the track's edge and the first and last item, in any CSS length (rem is a unit tied to the base text size). It's never less than 0.5rem, whatever you pass, because an edge item draws its focus ring there. Set it to the page gutter to run the track edge to edge.

props.name: className
props.description: Merged onto the region.

props.name: ref
props.description: Forwarded to the region.

keyboard.does: Moves to Previous, then Next, then through anything focusable in each item. An item scrolls into view as it takes focus.
On Previous or Next, scrolls one page of items. Does nothing (it's inert) at the matching end.
Scroll the track when the track itself has focus. The track is only a tab stop when no item holds anything focusable.

dos: Name it for what it holds: "Offers", "Top-rated accessories".
Give it enough items to scroll. Three that fit are a grid.
Link to the full list nearby. A carousel is a preview, so it shouldn't be the only way to reach the rest.
Set the gutter to the page gutter when the track should run to the edge of the page.
donts: Don't add autoplay. Content that moves on its own needs a pause control, and it pulls attention away from whoever's reading the page.
Don't put the only copy of anything in it. What's off to the side is easy to miss.
Don't hide the buttons on touch screens. A pointer, a switch device or a screen magnifier may be all someone has.
Don't wrap it in an element with overflow hidden to tidy the edges. That clips the focus ring the gutter is there to show.

anatomy.description: A section with aria-roledescription="carousel", named by the label. (ARIA, Accessible Rich Internet Applications, is a set of attributes that tell screen readers what an element is.)
Monospaced text such as "1 to 3 of 8", saying which items are showing. It updates on every scroll, but it isn't a live region, so screen readers don't read it out each time.
Secondary IconButtons, placed before the items in the Tab order. At the ends they're marked aria-disabled instead of disabled, so each stays a tab stop (a place the Tab key lands).
A list that's the browser's own scroll container, with scroll snap and no visible scrollbar. It's padded on all four sides, so an item at the edge draws its focus ring inside the track.
A list item, one per child, at the item width. The edge of the next one always shows.
Hidden from view, read by screen readers. Says where the track stopped after a press on Previous or Next.

components.name: ChartPanel
components.title: Chart panel
components.summary: One chart in a card. A sentence says what it shows, and the same numbers sit in a table. The data below is sample data.
components.useWhen: One chart (a line over time, bars by category, a donut of one whole, or a radar of several measures) with a summary sentence and the numbers as a table.
components.notFor: One number and its change: use Stat. One score from 0 to 100: use ScoreRing. Two measures on two scales: use two panels.

props.name: title
props.description: Required. The panel's heading and its name.

props.name: summary
props.description: Required. One sentence, the chart's caption.

props.name: kind
props.description: Required. Line for change over time. Bar to compare categories. Donut for parts of one whole (one series, a slice per row). Radar for several measures of one or two things (an axis per row).

props.name: data
props.description: Required. One object per category.

props.name: xKey
props.description: Required. The category. Its values must be unique.

props.name: xLabel
props.description: Required. The header of the table's first column.

props.name: series
props.description: Required. One or two series, coloured chart.series-1 then chart.series-2. Passing a third is a type error, and so is a ChartSeries.key that isn't one of Row's own numeric columns.

props.name: area
props.description: Line only. Fills under each line with a gradient of its colour that fades to nothing.

props.name: curve
props.description: Line only. smooth draws a monotone curve, so it never overshoots a data point.

props.name: grid
props.description: The dashed horizontal grid (on a radar, its web). false also drops the axis lines but keeps the tick labels.

props.name: size
props.description: sm is the stat-card size: a short sparkline with no axes or grid, and the caption under it. Pair it with headline.

props.name: headline
props.description: A formatted figure printed large under the title.

props.name: centerLabel
props.description: Donut only. The caption under the total in the centre of the ring.

props.name: formatValue
props.description: Formats numbers in the tooltip and the table. It formats the y-axis too, unless you give formatAxisValue.

props.name: formatAxisValue
props.description: Formats only the y-axis tick labels. Use a shorter, compact formatter when formatValue's output is too wide for the axis. SpendChart's compact euro formatter is one example.

props.name: axisWidth
props.description: The width the y-axis reserves, in px (pixels). 48 is Recharts' own YAxis default. Make it bigger if formatAxisValue's labels still get cut off.

props.name: bands
props.type: { from: string | number; to: string | number; label?: string }[]
props.description: Line and bar only. Shades stretches of the x-axis, such as night hours on a 24-hour chart. from and to are x-axis values (values of xKey), both included. When from comes after to in the data, the band wraps past the end: 22:00 to 06:00 shades 22:00 to the last point and the first point to 06:00. A band naming a value that isn't in the data is skipped. Every band is listed under the chart with its label, so screen readers hear it too.

props.name: limits
props.description: Line and bar only, not at size sm. Draws a dashed horizontal line at a y value, such as an alert limit of 35 µg/m³. The y-axis grows to include it, so a limit above every data point stays in view. Every limit is listed under the chart with its label and its value formatted by formatValue, so screen readers hear it too.

props.name: headingLevel
props.description: Pick the level that fits the page's heading outline.

props.name: className
props.description: Merged with the Card classes. Later Tailwind utilities win.

props.name: ref
props.description: Points at the section element.

Don't use a donut to compare categories over time. That's a job for a line or bars.

components.name: ChatThread
components.title: Chat thread
components.summary: A scrolling log of ChatMessages. It follows new text only while the reader is at the end, and it announces each finished reply to screen readers once.
components.useWhen: A conversation with an assistant, above a PromptInput, where replies stream in.
components.notFor: A record of events on one thing: use Timeline.
requires: A height, because the thread scrolls and the page doesn't. Use h-[28rem], or flex-1 min-h-0 inside a column.
ChatMessage children, so the thread can announce each finished reply.

props.name: label
props.description: Required. Names the log.

props.name: busy
props.description: The assistant is working. Shows a working line and makes one announcement when it starts.

props.name: busyLabel
props.description: The working line's words, and what gets announced.

props.name: jumpLabel
props.description: The jump button's words.

props.name: className
props.description: Goes on the root. Give the thread a height here.

keyboard.does: Moves to the log, then into the controls inside messages, then to Jump to latest when it's shown.
With the log focused, scrolls it.
With the log focused, scrolls it a page at a time.

dos: Give the thread a fixed or flexible height so the thread scrolls, not the page.
Set busy as soon as the request starts. Clear it when the last fragment has arrived or the reply is stopped.
After a Stop, add a system line ("Assistant stopped") so the record and the announcement both say what happened.
Keep the PromptInput outside the thread, directly under it.
donts: Don't scroll the thread yourself on new messages. It follows the end only while the reader is there.
Don't move focus into the thread when a reply arrives. Focus stays where the person put it.
Don't add a second live region (an area screen readers announce changes from) for replies or tool calls. The thread's status is the only voice.

pitfalls.why: A polite live log makes a screen reader read a streaming reply aloud one fragment at a time. The thread keeps the log quiet and announces each finished reply once.

pitfalls.right: <ChatThread ...>  // follows the end only while the reader is there
pitfalls.why: Scrolling on every change yanks away a reader who scrolled up to read. And smooth scrolling on every fragment means the screen never stops moving.

anatomy.description: Has role="log" and is named by label. aria-live is off, so screen readers don't read every change. It's a tab stop (a place the Tab key lands) so a keyboard can scroll it, and it scrolls inside its own height.
ChatMessage children, oldest first, 24px (pixels) apart.
Shown while busy: the conveyor Spinner and "Assistant is working" at the end of the log.
Appears only when the reader has scrolled away from the end. It jumps instantly and puts focus on the log.
A visually hidden role="status" that screen readers hear. It says the busy label once when work starts, and each finished reply once.

examples.caption: A live conversation: send anything, watch the reply stream in, press Stop to end it, or scroll up while it's still arriving

components.name: Dialog
components.title: Dialog
components.summary: A panel for one focused task, shown on top of the page. The page dims and goes inert, meaning it can't be clicked or focused. Keyboard focus moves inside the dialog and stays there. Escape or the close button hands focus back to whatever opened the dialog.
components.useWhen: A focused task on top of the page, such as an edit form.
components.notFor: A destructive confirm: use AlertDialog. A message that doesn't need a decision: use Toast.

props.name: open (Dialog)
props.description: Whether it is open, when your code controls that (controlled mode).

props.name: defaultOpen (Dialog)
props.description: Whether it starts open, when the component tracks its own state (uncontrolled mode).

props.name: onOpenChange (Dialog)
props.description: Called on every open and close, including Escape and a click on the scrim.

props.name: asChild (Trigger)
props.description: Uses its single child as the trigger instead of adding its own button. Pass a Button.

props.description: Required. The visible heading, and the name screen readers say.

props.name: description (Content)
props.description: Shown under the title. Screen readers read it as the accessible description.

props.name: size (Content)
props.description: Maximum width: 24rem, 32rem or 42rem (rem is a unit based on the root text size, usually 16 pixels).

props.name: closeLabel (Content)
props.description: What screen readers call the close button.

props.name: className (Content)
props.description: Added to the root classes. Where two Tailwind utility classes clash, the later one wins.

props.name: ref (Content)
props.description: The element with the role dialog.

props.name: ref (Trigger)
props.description: The trigger button.

props.name: asChild (Close)
props.description: Uses its single child as a control that closes the dialog.

props.name: className (Footer)
props.description: Added to the root classes. Where two Tailwind utility classes clash, the later one wins.

keyboard.does: Moves to the next control inside the dialog, looping from the last back to the first.
Moves back, looping from the first to the last.
Closes it and sends focus back to whatever opened it.

dos: Put the actions in DialogFooter. It lays them out in a row, aligned right, with the gap between buttons already set.
Write the body as plain elements inside DialogContent. It adds the padding and sets the body text (14px, meaning 14 pixels, in text.primary), so a bare paragraph already looks right.
Write the title as the task: 'Edit depot', not 'Edit'.
Put the safe action first in the footer.
Open it from a button, a trigger or a shortcut. Focus goes back to that control when it closes.
For long content with no field at the top, focus the panel itself when it opens (onOpenAutoFocus, tabIndex={-1}), not whatever button happens to come first.
donts: Don't open a dialog from a dialog. Finish or replace the first one.
Don't open one from a dropdown menu item. The item is gone by the time the dialog closes, so focus has nowhere to go back to.
Don't use one for a message that doesn't need a decision. That's a toast.

Don't check an untouched field on blur (when focus leaves it) in a dialog's form, and don't show ErrorSummary before a submit. The first field has focus when the dialog opens, so pressing Cancel blurs it first. An error appearing at that moment pushes the footer down mid-click, and Cancel never closes the dialog.

On the left. It's a container of its own: the grid below and the switch to an accordion both measure this section, so next to an aside the groups respond to the space they really have.
Optional, above the groups. Leave brand out when there is a wordmark, since the wordmark is the name.
Named by label, holding every group. It's one column while the link section is under 28rem wide (rem is a unit tied to the base text size), then two, three from 42rem and four from 48rem.
A heading in the monospaced face, in capitals, at the 11px (pixel) label size, followed by a slash. The slash is decoration and isn't part of any accessible name (the name a screen reader announces).

The same heading holds a button instead of text, with aria-expanded, aria-controls, a 44px height and a chevron. (ARIA, Accessible Rich Internet Applications, is a set of attributes that tell screen readers what a control does.) CSS shows one form and removes the other from the accessibility tree, the page structure screen readers read, so from 28rem up there's no button to announce.

Named by its title. Below 28rem a closed group's list is display: none, so it's out of the accessibility tree and out of the Tab order. Every group starts closed unless its defaultOpen says otherwise.

Before each link: one corner of the crosshair, 7px in size with a 1px line, in text.muted, sitting on the text baseline. When the link's hovered it takes the signal colour. It's aria-hidden, so screen readers skip it.
The Link atom's quiet tone at 14px, with a 24px target. An external link says it opens a new tab.

Only with aside. A heading drawn like a group title, then whatever you pass. It sits under the link section, and moves to its right at 21rem wide once the footer is 64rem wide. It isn't a landmark, because a form inside it already is one.
In text.muted at 12px, under a hairline and above the wordmark.

Only with wordmark. The name in the display face, bold and in capitals, exactly as wide as the footer at every width, with its foot cut off by the bottom edge. Nothing sits under it. It's an image named by the string, so it's announced once. Its box is sized from the letters alone, so it's already at its final size before the font loads.

Only with backdrop. A layer the full width of the footer behind the wordmark, with room above the letters so it can be seen. It's aria-hidden and ignores the pointer. Its height comes from the footer's width, so the space is there before the backdrop draws.

anatomy.description: The navigation region. Screen readers call it by the label prop.

A disclosure button (one that shows and hides the list) when the group can fold, plain text when it can't. It's text.secondary, so it still reads on a raised panel. Its list opens and closes by animating its height. Opening also fades and slides each item in, each one a little later than the one before (capped, so a long group never feels slow). Closing fades everything out together, all at once. If someone has asked their system for less motion (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce), both happen instantly.

An icon, a label and an optional count. The current page gets the fill, plus aria-current, an ARIA attribute (Accessible Rich Internet Applications, the labels screen readers rely on) that tells screen readers this is the page you are on.
